# On the Strange Beauty of Ordinary Moments

I've been thinking lately about how we move through the world mostly asleep, our attention scattered like loose change between work emails, social media feeds, and the perpetual background hum of things we should be doing. We have this idea that meaning lives in the mountaintop moments—graduations, weddings, that promotion we've been working toward for three years. But I'm increasingly convinced that the real texture of life, the stuff that actually makes it worth living, happens in spaces so mundane we barely notice them at all.

Yesterday morning, I sat in my kitchen for what I thought would be five minutes while my coffee brewed. The light was coming in at that particular angle that only happens in autumn, when the sun is lower and more golden, and it was hitting the side of my favorite mug in a way that made the ceramic seem almost luminous. I wasn't doing anything special—just standing there, waiting. And somewhere in that waiting, something shifted.

There's a Japanese concept called *kintsugi*, where broken pottery is repaired using gold, making the breaks visible and, in a strange way, more beautiful than the original. I think about this a lot. We're trained to hide our cracks, to sand them down, to present a version of ourselves that looks whole and unblemished. But what if the cracks are where the light gets in? What if that's not just nice poetry but actually true?

I know a woman—I'll call her Margaret—who worked in marketing for most of her life. She was good at it, wore the right clothes, said the right things, climbed the appropriate ladders. But she told me once, in that honest way people sometimes do after a glass of wine, that she spent thirty years in a career that never once made her feel truly alive. The money was fine. The status was fine. Everything was fine, except for the fundamental wrongness of spending the bulk of her waking life on something that didn't matter to her.

When she turned sixty, she quit. Not to pursue some glamorous dream—she didn't become a painter or move to Costa Rica or anything that would make a good Instagram post. She started a little garden. She learned to bake bread. She spent time with her grandchildren, not in that scheduled, activity-based way that modern parenting demands, but in the slow, aimless way of simply being together. She told me that baking bread has taught her more about patience and imperfection than anything else in her life. You can't rush dough. You can't force it. You have to work with its nature, feel the shifts in humidity and temperature, adjust accordingly. It's meditative. It's honest.

This is what I find myself returning to: the idea that we've organized modern life in a way that's fundamentally at odds with how humans actually thrive. We valorize productivity and optimization and disruption. We treat our bodies like machines that should never need downtime, our minds like computers that should be operating at maximum capacity at all times. We've turned rest into something you have to earn, rather than something essential to the basic machinery of being alive.

I'm not arguing for total rejection of ambition or structure. That would be naive. But I do think we've overcorrected, swung the pendulum so far toward constant achievement that we've made ourselves stranger to the texture of actual living.

There's something I've noticed about children before they're fully socialized into achievement culture. They notice things. A three-year-old will stop walking to observe an ant carrying something. They'll spend twenty minutes watching clouds move across the sky. They're not trying to be productive; they're just awake to the world in a way that seems, from the other side of adulthood, almost unimaginably precious.

Somewhere between childhood and adulthood, we lose this. We're trained to look through things rather than at them, to move quickly from moment to moment, always with an eye on what's next. The present becomes just a means to an end, never valuable in itself.

I wonder what would happen if we started building more space for the aimless. Not in that aspirational wellness way where meditation becomes another achievement to check off your list ("I meditated for 40 days straight"), but in a real, radical way. Time that has no outcome attached to it. Attention that doesn't need to produce anything.

There's this moment in the morning, after I've finished my coffee but before I really have to be anywhere, where I sometimes just sit. Not meditating, which implies a goal or technique I'm trying to master. Just sitting. Noticing what's happening—the quality of light, the sounds from the street, the texture of the chair against my back. It's almost embarrassingly simple, and yet it's become something I guard fiercely. Because I've noticed that the days when I protect this time are different. They're slower. I'm gentler with myself. Things don't feel quite so urgent.

I've been reading about the Japanese concept of *ma*—the space between things. In architecture, it refers to negative space. In music, it's the silence between notes. In conversation, it's the pause that lets meaning settle. The whole point is that emptiness isn't absence; it's full of potential. It's where things can breathe.

We don't build *ma* into our lives anymore. Every moment is filled with content, with purpose, with something that's supposed to be improving us or making us more productive. We've forgotten that emptiness might be valuable in itself.

I've also been thinking about how we relate to our own stories. We're encouraged to curate, to present a narrative that's coherent and compelling and preferably shows some kind of upward trajectory. But actual life is messier than that. It's full of false starts and side roads and periods where nothing much seems to be happening. We have moments of meaning tangled up with boredom and confusion and the simple fact of being alive without anything particularly interesting occurring.

And I think we're being cheated by the demand that everything be extraordinary. The ordinary *is* extraordinary, if you actually pay attention to it. The way light falls on a face you love. The specific taste of coffee made exactly the way you like it. The sound of someone you care about laughing in another room. These aren't lesser experiences than skydiving or traveling to exotic countries. They're just different. They're the texture of actual life.

One of the most important conversations I ever had happened in a car, stuck in traffic on a highway neither of us wanted to be on. There was nowhere to be, nothing to accomplish, so we just talked. Not about anything particularly grand—mostly small stuff, observations about people we knew, memories from childhood, things we'd been thinking about lately. But because there was no goal to the conversation, because we weren't trying to achieve anything, it went places that conversations rarely go. We said things we didn't know we were thinking until we said them.

I think about how that's almost impossible now. We're so structured. We have to carve out time for deep talks, schedule them, make them intentional. And intention is good, but there's something about accident, about stumbling into connection and meaning rather than planning for it, that feels vital.

My neighbor grows tomatoes. Just tomatoes, nothing else, in a small garden beside his house. He's retired, and from what I can tell, he spends the majority of his time tending to these plants. He waters them, talks to them, covers them with netting against the birds, adjusts the stakes as they grow. And then, when they're ripe, he gives them away. He doesn't sell them. He just hands them to neighbors, offers them to people walking by.

There's something radical about that. Spending months of work on something that will never make you money, just so you can give it away. It's almost obscene in its lack of productivity. And yet there's something deeply satisfying about it too. He seems genuinely happy. More happy, I'd wager, than people making six figures doing work they hate.

I think happiness might be less complicated than we've been told. Not easy, necessarily, but less complicated. It might be more about having time to be in your own life, less about having an impressive life to show to others. It might be about knowing the people around you, really knowing them. About noticing things. About doing work that feels like it means something, even if it doesn't mean anything to the world.

We've been sold this story where significance only comes from scale. You have to change the world, impact millions, build an empire. But what if significance just lives in showing up fully for the people in front of you? In making a meal someone enjoys. In being present during hard times. In noticing and appreciating the small beautiful things that are happening all the time.

The truth is, I don't know what the answer is. I'm still mostly caught in the same systems, the same anxieties as everyone else. I still check my email compulsively. I still feel that itch to be productive, that sense that time is slipping away and I should be accomplishing something. But I'm trying. I'm trying to build in more *ma*. More sitting. More noticing.

And what I've found is that this doesn't require dramatic changes. You don't have to quit your job or move to the woods (though if you want to, go ahead). You just have to occasionally say no to one more thing, so you can say yes to nothing in particular. You have to protect a little space where you're not trying to optimize or improve or achieve. Where you're just alive, just here, just paying attention.

Because that's where it is, I think. Not in the spectacular moments we're waiting for, but in the quiet ones we're trained to overlook. In the morning light. In the taste of good coffee. In the feeling of being fully present in a conversation with someone you care about. In the strange pleasure of watching an ant carry a crumb. In the spaces between, where nothing is happening and everything is.
